title: The Little Dog That Could Read
bodyHtml:
Sakata (also known as Kisakata or Kesakata) is a language in the Bantu family spoken by several thousand people in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. It consists of several quite distinct dialects; this problem features the dialect spoken in the village of Bosobe in the 1980s.

Below are some Sakata sentences, alongside their English translations. Note that ə and ü are both vowels, and that one Sakata noun is slightly irregular.

Banka balülü bamwi bebil benini.
The good women saw the big fields.
Banjir babibə badzo ibat lelülü.
The bad men killed the good duck.
Keto ketita kejo ntaw ne banjir.
The long snake heard the men's goat.
Mabat masinxunə ola mokan mo munjir.
The ducks wanted to eat the man's book.
Mva nekikə ne banka nejao otang.
The women's little dog learned to read.
Nə ala ipe le ibat lenini?
Who ate the big duck's wing?
Munkar nejo nko ne bang.
The woman heard the children's chicken.
Nko ibibə ila ncher i bang.
The bad chickens ate the children's peanuts.
Bande bachunga ntaw ilülü.
The white men bought the good goats.
Ntaw i banka ikwi o kebil ke munde.
The women's goats went to the white man's field.
Nə amwi bena be bande?
Who saw the white men's things?
Ngombe nekikə nemwi lecher lenini.
The little cow saw the big peanut.

Below are some numerical phrases in Sakata, alongside their English translations.

ledze lemo
one finger
ipyao lemo
one shoulder
nchungə ipə
two pigs
befwa besa
three bones
mete meni
four trees

questions.answerKey: Beto be kebil betang mekan menini.
acceptedVariants: Beto be kebil betang mekan menini

hints.text: Look at the first letter or two of each noun, then look at the first letter or two of every word that follows it in the same sentence. They keep matching. Sort the nouns into groups by how their neighbours start, and ignore meaning entirely while you do it.

Sakata sorts nouns into classes, and every adjective, verb and possessive linker that goes with a noun copies that noun's class marker. Singular and plural are different classes, so a word does not just change its own ending when it becomes plural — everything agreeing with it changes too. Build a table: noun class down the side, and the marker it forces on adjectives, verbs and linkers across the top.

Worked example: banka balülü bamwi bebil benini means the good women saw the big fields. Every word starts with be- or ba-. Now compare mva nekikə ne banka nejao — little dog, and everything agreeing with it starts ne-. So mva is in a different class from banka. Find mva again in G1a, where it is plural, and see which marker it takes there. Note that mva is the irregular noun the problem warns about.

explanationHtml:
Sakata is a Bantu language, and like most of the family it sorts every noun into a class. The class is not about meaning — it is closer to grammatical gender in French or German, except there are many more than two. What makes it visible is agreement: every adjective, verb and possessive linker attached to a noun copies that noun's class marker.

Reading a sentence

Take Banka balülü bamwi bebil benini — the good women saw the big fields. Almost every word starts with ba- or be-: banka (women) forces ba- on its adjective and verb, and bebil (fields) forces be- on its own adjective. Once you see that, the sentence parses itself.

The classes

ClassMarkerExample nounGloss
person sgmu- / ne-munjirman
person plba-banjirmen
thing sgke-kebilfield
thing plbe-bebilfields
long thing sgle- / lu-lecherpeanut
long thing pli-ncherpeanuts
mass sgmo-mokanbook
mass plme-mekanbooks
animal sgne-ngombecow
animal pli-ntawgoats

Notice that the noun itself often does not change between singular and plural — ntaw is goat and goats, ngombe is cow and cows. The number is carried entirely by what agrees with it. That is the single hardest idea in the problem, and it is why Mva imwi ntaw nebibə is the dogs saw the bad goat and not the reverse: imwi marks a plural subject, nebibə a singular one.

Possession

Possession is built with a linker that agrees with the thing possessed, not the possessor: ntaw i banka is goats of the women, where i matches ntaw. Compare kebil ke munde, field of the white man, where the linker matches kebil.

Numbers

Numerals agree too, which is what G3 tests. The root for one is -mo, for two -pə, three -sa, four -ni, and each takes the class prefix of the noun it counts. So one bone is kefwa kemo while three bones is befwa besa — the noun changes class between singular and plural, and the numeral follows it.

The title is a joke about the data: a little dog that learned to read is one of the sentences, and mva is the irregular noun the problem warns you about — it looks singular but takes plural agreement in some sentences.
